title: Only 10% Of The Population Can Pass This Grammar Quiz
summary: Sentence structure, verbs, punctuation and almost-correct wording get trickier across 10 fast rounds.

landing.intro: Think your grammar is flawless? Repair broken sentences, catch tiny punctuation traps and prove you can spot the mistake before it catches you.

about.body:
This worldwide grammar quiz turns everyday editing into ten increasingly difficult rounds. It covers sentence structure, verb forms, punctuation, apostrophes, pronoun clarity, modifier placement and the practical judgement needed to improve real notices, messages and short documents.

The challenge tests grammar shared across major standard-English varieties. It avoids spelling differences, optional punctuation styles, dialect traps and constructions where respected authorities accept more than one form, so every scored answer follows directly from the wording and register shown on screen.

Your final percentage reflects only the answers selected in this entertainment challenge. It is a playful snapshot of the language patterns you recognised most confidently, not a formal measure of English proficiency, education or professional editing ability.

howToPlay.title: How to Play
steps: Answer six questions in each proofreading round and choose the single option best supported by the sentence or document shown.
Correct answers stay hidden while you play, so inspect every verb, reference and punctuation mark before the quiz moves on.
Complete all ten rounds to reveal your Grammar Score, strongest skill and full answer-and-explanation review.

about.disclaimer: For entertainment and general learning only. This quiz is not a formal English-language assessment, academic qualification or proof of language proficiency.

score.disclaimer: For entertainment and general learning only. This quiz is not a formal English-language assessment, academic qualification or proof of language proficiency.

questions.question: Which option is a complete sentence?
answers: After the final paragraph
The editor checked the final paragraph.
Because the deadline changed
While everyone was waiting
questions.explanation: The second option contains a subject and a complete predicate, so it expresses a complete thought.

questions.question: Which sentence has correct subject–verb agreement?
answers: The list of corrections are on the desk.
The list of corrections were on the desk.
The list of corrections be on the desk.
The list of corrections is on the desk.
questions.explanation: The subject is the singular noun “list,” so it takes the singular verb “is.”

questions.context: The notes belong to several students.
questions.question: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
answers: The students’ notes were organised.
The student’s notes were organised.
The students notes’ were organised.
The students note’s were organised.
questions.explanation: For a regular plural noun ending in s, the possessive apostrophe follows the plural ending: “students’ notes.”

questions.context: Nora thanked Priya after Priya corrected the caption.
questions.question: Which revision makes the reference clearest?
answers: Nora thanked her after she corrected it.
She thanked Priya after she corrected it.
Nora thanked Priya for correcting the caption.
Nora thanked Priya after it was corrected by her.
questions.explanation: Naming the action and object removes any uncertainty about who corrected the caption.

questions.question: Which wording is the clearest and most concise?
answers: The report is concise in a clear manner.
The report is concise and clear.
The report has clarity and is concise in nature.
The report is being of a concise and clear kind.
questions.explanation: “Concise and clear” states both qualities directly without unnecessary wording.

questions.context: FORMAL NOTICE: Visitors must report to reception before entering the studio.
questions.question: Which version is clearest for the notice?
answers: Visitors, maybe report before entering.
Before entering it, reception is where visitors report.
Visitors report, to reception before entering the studio.
Before entering the studio, visitors must report to reception.
questions.explanation: The final version preserves the instruction, places the introductory phrase clearly and avoids ambiguity.

questions.context: The meeting ended early. The main speaker was ill.
questions.question: Which sentence combines the ideas correctly?
answers: The meeting ended early, the main speaker was ill.
Because the main speaker was ill. The meeting ended early.
The meeting ended early because the main speaker was ill.
The meeting because the main speaker was ill ended early and.
questions.explanation: The correct version joins the complete idea to its reason with the subordinating conjunction “because.”

questions.context: The two events happened at the same time; neither caused the other.
questions.question: Which sentence coordinates the ideas accurately?
answers: The lights flickered, and the presenter continued speaking.
Because the lights flickered, the presenter continued speaking.
The lights flickered, the presenter continued speaking.
The lights flickered although and the presenter continued.
questions.explanation: The coordinating conjunction “and” joins the simultaneous events without inventing a cause-and-effect relationship.

questions.question: Which sequence builds a clear sentence?

visual.ariaLabel: Although the rain stopped, unknown punctuation, the path remained slippery

answers: so but
and because
without punctuation
questions.explanation: A comma follows the introductory dependent clause before the main clause begins.

questions.question: Which option repairs the run-on sentence?
answers: The draft was ready, the printer had stopped.
The draft was ready, but the printer had stopped.
The draft was ready the printer, had stopped.
The draft was ready but. The printer had stopped.
questions.explanation: A comma plus the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins the two independent clauses.

questions.context: The paragraph describes two actions completed yesterday.
questions.question: Which sentence keeps the verb forms consistent?
answers: Mina opens the file and checked the figures.
Mina had opened the file and checks the figures.
Mina opened the file and checked the figures.
Mina opening the file and checked the figures.
questions.explanation: Both completed actions use the simple past: “opened” and “checked.”

questions.context:
EMAIL DRAFT
I reviewed the proposal. I have attached my notes. Please reply by Thursday.
questions.question: Which edit preserves three complete, clear sentences?
answers: I reviewed the proposal and attached my notes. Please reply by Thursday.
Reviewed the proposal, attached my notes. Please reply by Thursday.
I reviewed the proposal attached my notes, reply by Thursday.
Having reviewed. The proposal and my notes attached Thursday.
questions.explanation: The first edit combines related actions without losing a subject, finite verbs or the clear deadline.

questions.context: Timeline: 08:30 — Leo completed the chart. 09:00 — the meeting began.
questions.question: Which sentence expresses the order accurately?
answers: Leo completes the chart before the meeting began.
Leo was completing the chart after the meeting begins.
Leo has completed the chart after the meeting began.
Leo had completed the chart before the meeting began.
questions.explanation: The past perfect marks the earlier completed action, while the simple past marks the later meeting.

questions.context: Asha started at the library on Monday and still works there now.
questions.question: Which sentence matches the timeline?
answers: Asha worked at the library since Monday.
Asha has worked at the library since Monday.
Asha had worked at the library since Monday, but still does.
Asha is work at the library since Monday.
questions.explanation: The present perfect connects an action that began in the past with a situation that continues now.

questions.question: Which sentence has correct agreement?
answers: The final report, together with its appendices, are ready.
The final report, together with its appendices, be ready.
The final report, together with its appendices, is ready.
The final report, together with its appendices, being ready.
questions.explanation: The singular subject “report” takes the singular verb “is”; the intervening phrase about the appendices does not change the subject.

questions.question: Which sentence has correct agreement?
answers: Each of the reports contains a summary.
Each of the reports contain a summary.
Each of the reports containing a summary.
Each of the reports have contained a summary.
questions.explanation: The singular subject “each” takes the singular verb “contains.”

questions.context: The clause “which won the award” must describe the documentary, not the director.
questions.question: Which sentence attaches the clause clearly?
answers: The director, which won the award, introduced the documentary.
The director introduced, which won the award, the documentary.
Which won the award, the director introduced the documentary.
The director introduced the documentary, which won the award.
questions.explanation: Placing the relative clause directly after “the documentary” makes that noun its clear referent.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun correctly?
answers: The technicians completed the review by theirselves.
The technicians completed the review by themselves.
The technicians completed the review by themself.
The technicians completed themselves the review.
questions.explanation: The plural reflexive pronoun “themselves” refers back correctly to the plural subject “technicians.”

questions.question: Which sentence introduces the list correctly?
answers: Bring three items: a notebook, a pen and identification.
Bring: three items a notebook, a pen and identification.
Bring three: items, a notebook a pen and identification.
Bring three items; a notebook, a pen and identification.
questions.explanation: A colon can introduce a list after the complete clause “Bring three items.”

questions.context: The desks belong to two editors.
questions.question: Which phrase is punctuated correctly?
answers: the editor’s desks
the editors desks’
the editors’ desks
the editor’s’ desks
questions.explanation: The plural possessive “editors’” shows that the desks belong to more than one editor.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
answers: The file; because it was large, loaded slowly.
The file was large; it loaded slowly.
The file was; large and loaded slowly.
The file was large; and because loaded slowly.
questions.explanation: A semicolon correctly joins the two closely related independent clauses.

questions.question: Which sentence punctuates the introductory clause correctly?
answers: When the review ends send the file.
When, the review ends send the file.
When the review, ends send the file.
When the review ends, send the file.
questions.explanation: The comma separates the introductory dependent clause from the main instruction.

questions.context: Maya was walking into the room when she noticed the open window.
questions.question: Which sentence places the opening modifier clearly?
answers: Walking into the room, Maya noticed the open window.
Walking into the room, the open window caught Maya’s attention.
Maya noticed, walking into the room, the open window.
The room walking in, Maya noticed the window.
questions.explanation: Placing “Maya” directly after the opening modifier makes her the person who was walking.

questions.context:
NOTICE
For a clear formal notice, greet the host, sign the register and collect a badge.
questions.question: Which version is punctuated correctly?
answers: Greet the host sign the register, and collect a badge.
Greet, the host, sign the register and collect a badge.
Greet the host, sign the register and collect a badge.
Greet the host; sign the register, and collect a badge because.
questions.explanation: The commas separate the three parallel actions without introducing an incomplete clause.

questions.context: The policy has two sections. The second section contains the deadline.
questions.question: Which revision refers to the deadline most clearly?
answers: It contains it in the second one.
The policy has two sections, and it contains the deadline.
The deadline appears in the policy’s second section.
The second has it, which is in the policy.
questions.explanation: Naming both “deadline” and “second section” removes the competing possible references for “it.”

questions.context: The identity of the person who called is unknown.
questions.question: Which sentence is grammatical?
answers: The caller said that him would return.
The caller said that they would return.
The caller said that them would return.
The caller said that their would return.
questions.explanation: Singular “they” is a standard subject pronoun when the person’s identity is unknown.

questions.question: Which sentence keeps the plural reference clear?
answers: The folders were stacked, and it was labelled.
The folders was stacked, and they were labelled.
The folders were stacked, and he was labelled.
The folders were stacked, and they were labelled.
questions.explanation: The plural pronoun “they” correctly refers to the plural noun “folders,” and “were” maintains agreement.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the object pronoun correctly?
answers: Please send the draft to Lina and me.
Please send the draft to Lina and I.
Please send the draft to she and me.
Please send the draft to Lina and myself.
questions.explanation: After the preposition “to,” the object pronoun “me” is required.

questions.question: Which option is a complete, correctly ordered sentence?
answers: Because the labels were missing.
The labels, because missing, the boxes.
The boxes were delayed because the labels were missing.
The boxes because the labels were missing delayed.
questions.explanation: The correct option contains a complete main clause followed by a clear reason.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly punctuates a direct address?
answers: Ravi please, check the final line.
Ravi, please check the final line.
Ravi please check, the final line.
Ravi; please, check the final line.
questions.explanation: A comma separates the person being addressed directly from the rest of the sentence.

questions.context: Only the blue folders were archived; the other folders remained active.
questions.question: Which sentence preserves that restriction?
answers: The folders were archived blue only.
Only the folders were archived in blue.
The folders only were archived blue.
Only the blue folders were archived.
questions.explanation: Placing “only” directly before “the blue folders” restricts the action to that group and no other folders.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the precise comparison?
answers: The revised draft contains fewer errors than the first.
The revised draft contains less errors than the first.
The revised draft contains smallest errors than the first.
The revised draft contains fewest errors then the first.
questions.explanation: “Errors” is countable, so “fewer” is the appropriate comparative word.

questions.context: The intended meaning is that only Mira approved the second version; nobody else did.
questions.question: Which sentence expresses that meaning?
answers: Mira approved only the second version.
Only Mira approved the second version.
Mira only approved the second version.
Mira approved the second version only yesterday.
questions.explanation: Placing “only” directly before “Mira” makes her the sole person who approved it.

questions.question: Which comparison is complete and clear?
answers: This guide explains the process more clear.
This guide more clearly explains than the old one does it.
This guide explains the process more clearly than the old one does.
This guide explains more clearly the old one.
questions.explanation: The adverb “clearly” modifies “explains,” and the comparison names both items.

questions.question: Which sentence has correct agreement?
answers: The set of instructions are easy to follow.
The set of instructions were easy to follow now.
The set of instructions be easy to follow.
The set of instructions is easy to follow.
questions.explanation: The head noun “set” is singular, so it takes the singular verb “is.”

questions.context: EMAIL GOAL: Ask the team to submit one final file by 17:00.
questions.question: Which sentence is clearest?
answers: Please submit the final file by 17:00.
Please, submit finally the file somewhere around 17:00 maybe.
The final file should have submission by the team in a final way.
By 17:00, a file final the team submits please.
questions.explanation: The first option gives one direct action and an unambiguous deadline.

questions.context:
EMAIL DRAFT
The schedule changed. Please review the new times. Reply if any time is impossible.
questions.question: Which subject line best matches the message?
answers: Something Happened
Action Required: Review the Revised Schedule
A Very Long Message About Different Things
No Reply Needed
questions.explanation: The correct subject line names the change and the action the reader must take.

questions.context:
NOTICE DRAFT
Visitors must signing in, wear a badge and returning it before leaving.
questions.question: Which edit makes the list parallel?
answers: Visitors must signing in, wearing a badge and return it.
Visitors must signed in, wear a badge and returned it.
Visitors must sign in, wear a badge and return it before leaving.
Visitors signing in, badge wearing and it returns.
questions.explanation: “Sign,” “wear” and “return” use matching base forms after “must.”

questions.context:
PARAGRAPH
The room was ready. Except for the missing chairs. The guests arrived at noon.
questions.question: Which edit removes the fragment?
answers: The room was ready except for the missing chairs. The guests arrived at noon.
The room was ready. Except the missing chairs were. The guests arrived.
The room. Was ready except for missing chairs, guests arrived.
Except for the missing chairs. The room was ready and at noon.
questions.explanation: Attaching the exception to the complete sentence removes the fragment without changing the meaning.

questions.context: The intended meaning is that the speaker answered nearly every question.
questions.question: Which wording expresses that meaning?
answers: The speaker answered every nearly question.
Nearly the speaker answered every question.
The speaker nearly answered every question.
The speaker answered nearly every question.
questions.explanation: “Nearly” sits directly before “every,” showing that almost all questions were answered.

questions.context: The second clause explains the first.
questions.question: Which punctuation is correct?
answers: The deadline moved; because the client requested more time.
The deadline moved: the client requested more time.
The deadline: moved the client requested more time.
The deadline moved, the client requested more time.
questions.explanation: The complete first clause can introduce its explanation with a colon.

questions.context: A report contains a summary and an appendix. The appendix is updated monthly.
questions.question: Which edit makes the monthly update refer to the appendix?
answers: The report contains a summary and an appendix, and it is updated monthly.
It contains a summary and an appendix that is updated monthly by it.
The report contains a summary and an appendix; the appendix is updated monthly.
The report, updated monthly, contains a summary and its appendix.
questions.explanation: Repeating “the appendix” removes uncertainty about whether the report, summary or appendix receives the update.

questions.question: Choose the correct coordination.
answers: The doors opened, but nobody entered.
The doors opened, nobody entered.
Although the doors opened, but nobody entered.
The doors opened but. Nobody entered.
questions.explanation: A comma and “but” correctly join the two contrasting independent clauses.

questions.question: Which verb agrees?
answers: On the desk is three revised pages.
On the desk be three revised pages.
On the desk was three revised pages.
On the desk are three revised pages.
questions.explanation: In the inverted sentence, the plural subject “three revised pages” takes the plural verb “are.”

questions.context: The handle belongs to one door.
questions.question: Choose the correct apostrophe.
answers: the doors handle
the doors’ handle
the door’s handle
the door’ handle
questions.explanation: The singular possessive “door’s” shows that the handle belongs to one door.

questions.question: Choose the reflexive pronoun.
answers: The designers prepared the display by theirselves.
The designers prepared the display by themselves.
The designers prepared the display by themself.
The designers prepared the display by theirs.
questions.explanation: The plural reflexive pronoun “themselves” correctly refers back to “the designers.”

questions.context: The number almost doubled but did not quite reach twice its original size.
questions.question: Which wording matches?
answers: The update nearly doubled the number.
The update doubled nearly the number.
Nearly the update doubled the number.
The update doubled the nearly number.
questions.explanation: “Nearly” directly modifies “doubled,” showing that the increase fell just short of doubling.

questions.question: Which formal edit works?
answers: Send it soon-ish.
The file, send whenever.
Sending of file is wanted.
Please send the file by noon.
questions.explanation: The final option gives a clear action and deadline in concise formal language.

questions.question: Which sentence handles the contrast correctly?
answers: The storm ended; although the streets remained flooded.
The storm ended, however the streets remained flooded.
Although the storm ended; the streets remained flooded.
Although the storm ended, the streets remained flooded.
trapdoorErrors: semicolon incorrectly separates a main clause from a dependent clause
conjunctive adverb lacks the required boundary punctuation
semicolon incorrectly follows a dependent clause
questions.explanation: The dependent clause beginning with “although” is followed by a comma and a complete main clause.

questions.context:
STATUS
One final title is ready. Three revised captions are also ready.
questions.question: Which sentence has correct agreement?
answers: Three revised captions, as well as the final title, is ready.
Three revised captions, as well as the final title, be ready.
Three revised captions, as well as the final title, are ready.
Three revised captions, as well as the final title, being ready.
trapdoorErrors: singular verb does not agree with the plural subject
base form cannot stand alone as the finite verb
non-finite form leaves the sentence incomplete
questions.explanation: The plural subject “captions” takes “are”; the intervening phrase beginning with “as well as” does not change that agreement.

questions.context: The company owns the policy, and it is currently updating the handbook.
questions.question: Which sentence uses both forms correctly?
answers: The company changed it’s policy because its updating the handbook.
The company changed its policy because it’s updating the handbook.
The company changed its’ policy because its updating the handbook.
The company changed it’s policy because it’s updating the handbook.
trapdoorErrors: possessive and contraction are both reversed
invalid possessive form and missing contraction
questions.explanation: Possessive “its” has no apostrophe, while “it’s” correctly contracts “it is.”

questions.context: The manager assigned the final check to Priya and the speaker.
questions.question: Which pronoun completes the sentence?
answers: The manager assigned the final check to Priya and me.
The manager assigned the final check to Priya and I.
The manager assigned the final check to Priya and myself.
The manager assigned the final check to Priya and mine.
trapdoorErrors: subject form used as the object of a preposition
reflexive form has no matching antecedent
independent possessive used as an object
questions.explanation: The pronoun is an object of the preposition “to,” so the object form “me” is required.

questions.context: The editor revised the first report, not the other reports.
questions.question: Which sentence preserves that exact meaning?
answers: Only the editor revised the first report.
The editor revised the first report only to correct the title.
The editor revised the first report only yesterday.
The editor revised only the first report.
trapdoorErrors: only changes who performed the action
the purpose phrase changes why the report was revised
only changes when the action happened
questions.explanation: Placing “only” immediately before “the first report” restricts the revision to that report.

questions.context:
NOTICE GOAL
The east entrance is closed. Direct visitors to the north entrance.
questions.question: Which notice is clear and grammatical?
answers: With the east entrance closed, visitors should use north entrance.
The east entrance is closed; visitors uses the north entrance.
The east entrance is closed; visitors should use the north entrance.
Visitors should use the north entrance, the east entrance is closed.
trapdoorErrors: missing article before a singular countable entrance
questions.explanation: The semicolon joins two complete related clauses, and the instruction uses correct agreement and the required article.

questions.context:
FACTS
The exhibition opened late. Even so, hundreds of visitors arrived before noon.
DRAFT
The exhibition opened late, hundreds of visitors arrived before noon.
questions.question: Which edit fixes the structure and preserves the contrast?
answers: The exhibition opened late because hundreds of visitors arrived before noon.
Although the exhibition opened late, hundreds of visitors arrived before noon.
The exhibition opened late, and therefore hundreds arrived before noon.
Opening late, hundreds of visitors were the exhibition before noon.
questions.explanation: “Although” repairs the comma splice and preserves the stated contrast rather than inventing a cause.

questions.context:
TIMELINE
10:00 — the team completed the checks.
10:30 — the doors opened.
The account is written from 11:00.
questions.question: Which sentence reports the order correctly?
answers: The team had completed the checks before the doors opened.
The team completes the checks after the doors opened.
The team has complete the checks before the doors open yesterday.
The team were completed the checks after opening.
questions.explanation: The past perfect marks the earlier completed checks, while the simple past marks the later opening.

questions.context:
NOTICE DRAFT
Bring the following items a notebook, identification and your booking confirmation.
questions.question: Which edit correctly introduces and punctuates the list?
answers: Bring: the following items, a notebook identification and your booking confirmation.
Bring the following items; a notebook, identification and your booking confirmation.
Bring the following items, a notebook; identification and your booking confirmation.
Bring the following items: a notebook, identification and your booking confirmation.
questions.explanation: The complete introductory clause ends with a colon, and commas separate the three listed items.

questions.context:
FORM DRAFT
Each applicant should attach your receipt and keep their original.
REGISTER
The form uses formal third-person instructions throughout.
questions.question: Which edit makes the reference and register consistent?
answers: Each applicant should attach your receipt and keep your original.
Applicants should attach his receipt and keep their original.
Each applicant should attach their receipt and keep the original.
Each applicant should attach our receipt and keep its original.
questions.explanation: Singular “their” is standard English, maintains third-person reference and avoids the draft’s shift to second person.

questions.context:
INTENDED MEANING
The guide explains the process more clearly than the earlier guide. It does not contain more information.
questions.question: Which sentence preserves both clues?
answers: The new guide explains more information than the earlier guide.
The new guide explains the process more clearly than the earlier guide.
The new guide more explains clearly information than earlier.
Clearly, the new guide contains more process information.
questions.explanation: The correct option compares clarity, not quantity, and places the adverb “clearly” with the verb it modifies.

questions.context:
EMAIL DRAFT
The venue changed to Hall B. The start time remains 14:00. Please confirm that you received this update.
questions.question: Which revision communicates every required detail clearly?
answers: The venue is now Hall B, the start time remains 14:00, and please confirm receipt of this update.
Something changed, but the time did not. Reply.
Hall B is at 14:00 because confirmation changed the venue.
Please confirm the venue, which is changing the time to Hall B.
questions.explanation: The first revision retains the new venue, unchanged time and request for confirmation in a clear grammatical sentence.
